h1: Whisky for legal and compliance teams
title: Whisky for Legal and Compliance Teams | Craft Beer School
desc: The whisky product knowledge legal and compliance teams need: category definitions, label terms, excise movements and advertising limits.
teaser: Compliance in a whisky company starts with knowing what the words on the label mean on the distillery floor.
standfirst: Legal and compliance teams in spirits companies review labels, campaigns, contracts and excise filings. Each one depends on product facts: what makes a whisky a single malt, what an age statement promises, why stock cannot cross a state border. This guide gives those facts at process level.
sections:
Many whisky terms have legal definitions in the country of origin. Scotch must be distilled and matured in Scotland for at least three years in oak casks and bottled at a minimum of 40% ABV. Bourbon must be made in the United States from at least 51% corn, distilled to no more than 80% ABV and filled at no more than 62.5% ABV into new charred oak containers. Irish whiskey must mature at least three years on the island of Ireland.

In India, FSSAI standards for alcoholic beverages describe whisky, malt whisky and blended products. A product imported in bulk and bottled in India may carry origin claims only within the rules of both countries. Compliance teams should read the current standards rather than relying on how competitors label.

Some words create promises the liquid must keep:

  • Age statement: the age of the youngest whisky in the bottle, not an average.
  • Single malt: malted barley whisky from a single distillery.
  • Blended: a mix of whiskies, or in India often of malt spirit with neutral spirit.
  • Cask strength: bottled without reduction to a standard strength, or close to it.
  • Small batch and reserve: often undefined, so claims must match what the company can show.

Our guide to the whisky label compliance review walks through a full label check.
Every movement is an excise event

Spirit in an Indian distillery sits under excise control from production onward. Movement into bond, reduction, bottling, dispatch and transfer to another state all need permits or records under state excise rules. Duty is usually paid when goods leave bond for sale in a state.

For legal teams, this means contracts for bottling, contract distilling or bulk purchase must reflect who holds the licence at each stage and who bears duty. A supply agreement that ignores the permit timeline can promise deliveries that are not legally possible. Rules vary by state and change, so the compliance team should map current requirements for each state the company operates in.
Advertising limits shape the whole business

Direct advertising of alcohol is restricted in India. Brands have used brand extensions such as soda, water or music CDs under the same name, which raises questions of surrogate advertising. Our guide to surrogate advertising rules covers the debate.

Inside the company, legal reviews every campaign, social post and event. The common tests are whether the content promotes alcohol directly, whether it could appeal to people under the legal drinking age and whether it links drinking with success, driving or health. The legal drinking age itself differs between states, which matters for events and digital targeting.

A distillery produces a stream of records: batch sheets, lab analyses, cask registers, bottling logs. Many are required by excise or food law. All of them become evidence if a product is questioned. Methanol, for instance, is a regulated contaminant in spirits. Labs test for it as routine.

Legal teams should know where these records live, how long they are kept and who signs them. When a complaint or a regulator's query arrives, the ability to trace a bottle back to its batch and casks is what lets the company respond quickly.

Statutory warnings on labels, age checks at events, limits on sponsorship and careful wording in campaigns all come from the same principle. A whisky company's licence to operate depends on it. Internal tastings and training should follow the same rules: opt-in, small measures, water and spit cups, nobody driving afterwards and non-drinkers fully included.

Compliance teams who understand the product can explain the reasons behind rules, which makes colleagues far more likely to follow them.
What your team gains from knowing the product

Lawyers who have seen a cask warehouse read an age claim differently. Compliance officers who understand distillation cuts know why methanol testing matters. A short guided session on the product, with a responsible, opt-in nosing, gives legal teams the vocabulary to challenge marketing claims with confidence. This guide is process knowledge, not legal advice.

A practical first step: take your three best-selling labels and list every descriptive word on each. Mark which are legally defined, which are company claims and which need evidence on file.
faqs: Is an age statement an average age?
No. It refers to the youngest whisky in the bottle.
Why do whisky contracts need excise detail?
Every movement of spirit needs permits or records under state excise rules, so contracts must match who holds the licence and pays duty at each step.
No. It explains product facts and processes. Rules vary by state and change, so check current notifications and take legal advice.
